title: She killed his sister and her family while driving drunk. Now they're speaking together about forgiveness
summary: In 2016 Catherine McKay killed a family of four in a car collision outside of Saskatoon. A court later heard her blood alcohol was three times the legal limit.

image.caption: Chad Mierau and Catherine McKay on Friday, Nov. 27 in Tisdale, Saskatchewan. McKay killed Mierau's sister and her family in 2016 while she was driving impaired. (Maeve Ellis)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan
In 2016 Catherine McKay killed a family of four in a car collision outside of Saskatoon. A court later heard her blood alcohol was three times the legal limit.
Catherine McKay, Chad Mierau speak about healing, forgiveness ten years after crash that killed family of four
Chad Mierau remembers when he first met with the woman who killed his sister and her family.
"Those conversations were beautiful. They were heartfelt. They were full of tears. The first one it was really hard to make eye contact. We both had a heck of a lot of stuff going on," he said.
In 2016 Catherine McKay killed his sister and her family of four in a car collision outside of Saskatoon. A court later heard her blood alcohol was three times the legal limit.
Now they're speaking publicly together about the power of forgiveness and healing trauma.
"It was important for me to have her know that I forgive her. It was for me. It was something I had to do. It was my healing journey. I had to set some things down. It was so heavy," he said.
Their first two talks in a series of public conversations were on Friday in Tisdale, a town of about 3,000 in central Saskatchewan. They spoke with students and then a group of about 15.

blocks.text: Chanda Van de Vorst, her husband, Jordan, and their two children, Miguire, 2, and Kamryn, 5, died when McKay drove through an intersection just outside Saskatoon. She later pleaded guilty and received a nine-year sentence.

Jordan Van de Vorst, 34, his wife, Chanda, 33, and their two children, Kamryn, 5, and Miguire, 2, all died after a drunk driving crash at the corner of Highway 11 and Wanuskewin Road north of Saskatoon in January 2016. (Submitted by Chad Mierau)
Mierau remembers the junior RCMP officer who first called couldn't bring himself to say the full impact.

blocks.text: "The hardest part beyond the hospital was the house. They literally just went to Costco the day of the accident. The fridge was full of groceries," he said.
He remembers the initial hours of confusion in the hospital.
"You're trying to figure out what is my new normal? What does my new life look like without four of my favourite people?," he said.
Chad Mierau poses for a photograph with his five-year-old niece, Kamryn Van de Vorst and two-year-old nephew, Miguire, before they were killed in a drunk driving crash. (Submitted by Chad Mierau)
McKay said that when an officer told her she killed someone, she couldn't believe it.

"None of us ever think that we can possibly be that person. I mean anybody, friends or people that knew me well would have told you, six months, a year before that, 'there's no way that would be her,'" she said.

"That's part of the reason I'm here is that it's really important for you to realize that this could easily happen. So easily that you could be literally sitting in a jail cell and go 'I don't understand,'" she said.
Mierau said he reached out to McKay's daughter in a long message when he saw hatred against the family on Facebook.
"I said 'I really want to reach out to your mom and tell her I forgive her,'" he said, as McKay was still detained.
"I have people question me quite often, 'How do you do that? How do you find forgiveness for someone that's taken four family members?' and I don't really know how to put that into words."
Chad Mierau grieves "four of his favourite people" after McKay went through a stop sign and killed his sister, her husband, and their two kids in January 2016. (Chanss Lagaden/CBC)
McKay remembers sleepless nights and years of suicidal thoughts. She eventually found part of her path to recovery in a healing lodge while she was carrying out her sentence.
"Before all of this happened I was basically an atheist. I had no beliefs, I had no spirituality at all, which was part of the reason I was so sick. I didn't feel that there was any hope," she said.
They spoke about the importance of healing trauma to prevent ongoing harm.
McKay said she experienced sexual abuse as a child and only sought help for it as an adult. As a single mother of five, she fell into alcoholism.
"I didn't take care of problems. I didn't take care of the trauma I'd been through. I didn't reach for help. I reached for a bottle," she said.
Son of drunk driver who killed family says he was 'destroyed and heartbroken' by what his mother did

McKay said alcohol is too prevalent and encouraged in Saskatchewan, and she had her first drink when she was 10. She said she's particularly upset about the rising rates of highway fatalities in the province.

"I don't know why I'm here but I do know that because I'm here that there's something that I'm supposed to be doing and I'm supposed to make a difference so this doesn't happen to anybody else," she said. "So there doesn't have to be another family like Chad's that has to pay the ultimate price for someone that didn't take care of their shit."

blocks.text: Mierau said his life will never be the same afterwards. Old business ventures like his rental properties are off his mind.
"If Catherine and I can lean on each other as we heal, surely to God, other people can lean on their neighbours," said Mierau.
Mierau said he hopes that them speaking together would make their message more profound.
"It can have a bigger impact if we combine efforts to do this and for me that's the big picture," he said.
